kind: r/mcp · 作者直接回复我方并采纳建议 · 第二轮往返
context: r/mcp api2ai showcase 帖第二轮。我方首评指出『metadata 里声明的每个能力都是某个客户端会来考你的契约』并点名 MCP annotations（readOnlyHint/destructiveHint/openWorldHint）是 OpenAPI 无处安放的东西。作者 annette_dorothea 回复表示这个 framing 帮助很大，明确说 annotations 要加进 DSL 待办、并说『你的评论说服了我它们应该被支持』，同时给出 DSL 语法和 hooks 分层设计（OpenAPI 是 paths/schemas/validation 的 source of truth，DSL 负责 opt-in 与 agent 向元数据，hooks 负责运行时行为）。我方要接的下一层：annotations 将是她 DSL 里唯一一个无法对 OpenAPI 验证的字段——其他字段都有 spec 兜底，annotation 是纯声明，声明与实现会静默漂移。我方真实做法：把全部 15 个工具的公开面（名称、参数、默认值、枚举、annotations）冻结在一个契约测试里，加工具就让构建失败直到有人显式更新，已经拦下两次会静默发给已安装客户端的破坏性变更；但那份 pin 是手写的，是真相的副本而不是真相。目标：给她一个正在做的事情的具体设计难点，保持同行关系。
reader: Thanks, that framing helped a lot. Especially the point that every capability you declare becomes a contract some client may enforce. That's exactly why I don't want a blind OpenAPI dump: generation can easily advertise things you never consciously chose to support. And thanks for calling out MCP annotations. destructiveHint, readOnlyHint, and similar annotations are going on my list. You're right: HTTP verbs aren't enough, OpenAPI has nowhere honest to express them, and clients actually use them. In api2ai, the OpenAPI specification remains the source of truth for paths, schemas, and validation. The AI layer is a small DSL that opts in operations and overlays agent-facing metadata. Nothing becomes a tool unless you explicitly declare it. Hooks are a separate layer for project-specific runtime behavior (authorization, filling customerId from a JWT, reshaping responses, etc.). They aren't where annotations belong. So my view is that annotations belong in the DSL alongside intent and summary as explicit curation, not inferred from HTTP methods and not hidden in hooks. They're not supported yet, but your comment convinced me they should be.
draft:
Putting them in the DSL rather than the hooks is the right call, and I think the reason is harder than metadata belonging next to metadata. Annotations have to exist at tools/list time, before any call happens, because that's the moment a client reads destructiveHint and decides whether to interrupt the user. A hook runs far too late to matter there.

What your design gets that mine doesn't is that the declaration can be the source of truth instead of a copy of it. I froze my whole public surface in a test file, every tool name, parameter, default and annotation, so adding a tool fails the build until someone updates the pin deliberately. It's caught two breaking changes that would have gone out silently to already-installed clients. But I typed that pin by hand. It's a copy. Copies drift. Yours could generate it.

One data point while you're deciding the shape. Of my fifteen tools exactly one is flagged destructive, and getting there meant restructuring rather than annotating, since updates became versioned upserts and cancel became a recorded state instead of a delete. The annotation is what told me my design was wrong. I didn't expect that from a metadata field.
